                'Give me a child until he is seven, and I will give you the man.' This Jesuit motto has opened every episode of director Michael Apted's ground-breaking Up series, which has endeavoured to catch up with the same 14 people every seven years since 1964, when they were seven years old. Now, in the final show - without Apted, who died in 2021 - those children are 70. So as they look back on their lives, does that adage still ring true? No one is untouched by change. Some have had happy lives, others not so much. Bruce Balden was at boarding school when he was chosen, and he became a teacher. 'I do see myself in that seven-year-old,' he says. 'I don't know whether some aspects of my character are immutable or I've changed. But I see a rather lost soul. I want to reassure him that it will be a ride, but life is going to be all right.' Seven-year-old Bruce just wanted to see his father, a soldier in Southern Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe). Now he reads a poem in which his dad explains his feelings for his son. </script> <!-- CWV --><div itemprop="articleBody"><p class="mol-para-with-font">The grieving sister of an 18-year-old sixth form student killed by meningitis B has issued a plea begging others to get vaccinated against the deadly disease.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Nicole Zographou's baby brother George had excitedly set off to the Boardmasters surf and music festival in Newquay, but told his sister he was feeling ill beforehand.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Undeterred and determined to enjoy himself, young George and his friend drove off from Bristol, but on the journey his condition worsened.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">He developed a pain in his foot and became increasingly woozy. Overnight, he began uncontrollably vomiting and could no longer walk by morning.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Unbeknownst to him, a meningococcal infection was ripping through his body at terrifying speed.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Hours later, he collapsed, suffering a heart attack and a catastrophic brain injury. He was rushed to hospital, where he was found to be a victim of meningitis B - a vicious bug which cruelly targets teenagers and young adults.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Five days on, his family was forced to make the brutal decision to turn off his life support. Sparkly-eyed, kind, funny, beautiful George was dead.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Nicole, 38, said: 'He died in his peak. If George hadn't got meningitis B, he would be with us today. He would be 28, enjoying a good career, having finished university, and still be having fun.</p><div class="artSplitter mol-img-group" style="style"> <div class="mol-img"> <div class="image-wrap"> <img id="i-79569ce67da40c07" src="https://i.dailymail.com/1s/2026/09/13/09/111217227-16127457-image-a-1_1789287361404.jpg" height="422" width="634" alt="Nicole Zographou said her 18-year-old brother's death from meningitis B 'has bled into every part of my life.' She added: 'We were really close, and I miss him incredibly'" class="blkBorder img-share" style="max-width:100%" loading="lazy" /> </div> </div> <p class="imageCaption">Nicole Zographou said her 18-year-old brother's death from meningitis B 'has bled into every part of my life.' She added: 'We were really close, and I miss him incredibly'</p></div><div class="artSplitter mol-img-group" style="style"> <div class="mol-img" style="height: auto;"> <div class="image-wrap"> <img id="i-1f46a3d5a86ddb63" src="https://i.dailymail.com/1s/2026/09/13/09/111217119-16127457-Nicole_a_senior_public_health_practitioner_urged_young_people_to-a-22_1789288212978.jpg" height="573" width="634" alt="Nicole, a senior public health practitioner, urged young people to get vaccinated. She said: 'Please check. Please ask. Please have the jabs and get protected. Please don't make the mistake of thinking this won't happen to you.'" class="blkBorder img-share" style="max-width:100%" loading="lazy" /> </div> </div> <p class="imageCaption">Nicole, a senior public health practitioner, urged young people to get vaccinated. She said: 'Please check. Please ask. Please have the jabs and get protected. Please don't make the mistake of thinking this won't happen to you.'</p></div><p class="mol-para-with-font">'His death has bled into every part of my life. We were really close, and I miss him incredibly. I'd give the world to have him back.' </p><p class="mol-para-with-font">The coroner's reports stated that the only thing that would have saved George's life would have been a vaccination, senior public health practitioner Nicole said.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">She issued an urgent warning for students to get vaccinated ahead of the return to university later this month.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">In a desperate plea, she added: 'Please check. Please ask. Please have the jabs and get protected. Please don't make the mistake of thinking this won't happen to you.' </p><p class="mol-para-with-font">In March, two students aged 18 and 21 were killed by meningitis B in an outbreak in Kent which <a style="font-weight: bold;" target="_self" href="/news/article-15651395/Fears-Kent-meningitis-outbreak-bigger-medics-realised-Second-party-linked-cases-student-coma-two-dead.html">infected 21 people following a fateful club night out</a>. Another 18-year-old was killed in Oxfordshire by the disease in May.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Last week, the teenagers in Suffolk were rushed to hospital with the same infection.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Nicole spoke further about her brother's death in 2017: 'George felt a little unwell. Five days later he was dead. That is how quickly this disease can take hold.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'You cannot look at a healthy 18-year-old and imagine that they could be dead within days. That's what is so frightening about meningitis.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'It can start with symptoms that seem ordinary, and you might not realise how seriously ill someone is until they suddenly deteriorate so quickly that they cannot be treated.' </p><div class="artSplitter mol-img-group" style="style"> <div class="mol-img"> <div class="image-wrap"> <img id="i-d37a3e5099b37988" src="https://i.dailymail.com/1s/2026/09/13/09/111217117-16127457-image-a-3_1789287511153.jpg" height="1279" width="634" alt="George Zographou said he had been feeling mildly ill before he set off to Boardmasters festival in 2017. Five days later his family were forced to shut off his life support after he was struck down by meningitis" class="blkBorder img-share" style="max-width:100%" loading="lazy" /> </div> </div> <p class="imageCaption">George Zographou said he had been feeling mildly ill before he set off to Boardmasters festival in 2017. Five days later his family were forced to shut off his life support after he was struck down by meningitis</p></div><div class="artSplitter mol-img-group" style="style"> <div class="mol-img"> <div class="image-wrap"> <img id="i-48b2f8bb6e31077" src="https://i.dailymail.com/1s/2026/09/13/09/111217033-16127457-image-a-5_1789287572518.jpg" height="845" width="634" alt="Nicole said: 'There were four of us in our happy family. Now we’re like a three-legged chair and we don’t really function very well any more without him'" class="blkBorder img-share" style="max-width:100%" loading="lazy" /> </div> </div> <p class="imageCaption">Nicole said: 'There were four of us in our happy family. Now we’re like a three-legged chair and we don’t really function very well any more without him'</p></div><div class="artSplitter mol-img-group" style="style"> <div class="mol-img"> <div class="image-wrap"> <img id="i-47997971ef549090" src="https://i.dailymail.com/1s/2026/09/13/09/111217057-16127457-image-a-23_1789288225379.jpg" height="907" width="634" alt="Nicole added: 'The coroner's report said the only thing that would have saved him was a vaccination. That's what it said on his on his death report.'" class="blkBorder img-share" style="max-width:100%" loading="lazy" /> </div> </div> <p class="imageCaption">Nicole added: 'The coroner's report said the only thing that would have saved him was a vaccination. That's what it said on his on his death report.'</p></div><p class="mol-para-with-font">Nicole painfully recalled the day she last saw her brother - a student at St Brendon's Sixth Form College in Bristol - before he was struck down by meningitis.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">George was excited - excited for his first festival experience, even excited by the journey, having never driven on a motorway before.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">She said: 'He told me he was feeling a little unwell and I advised him not to push himself. I told him to make sure he sought help if he needed it, but he wasn't feeling too bad, so none of us were too worried.'</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Nicole was jetting off to Ibiza for a week on her own adventure, which she had been really looking forward to as well. So they said their goodbyes and parted ways.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Soon after arriving in Newquay, George was texting their parents -mum Elaine, now 73, and dad Andrew Zographou, now 59 - and Snapchatting Nicole in Ibiza to tell them he had started feeling very unwell. </p><p class="mol-para-with-font">The following evening, a call came that changed the family forever. George had gone into cardiac arrest and stopped breathing for 12 minutes.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Nicole said: 'From the call, I learned he'd been blue-lighted to hospital, placed on life support and was found to have suffered a catastrophic brain injury.'</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">She rushed back home, getting the first flight back from Ibiza and arrived 10 hours later at her brother's side, where he was being kept alive with a life support machine.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Nicole continued: 'He was catastrophically brain dead. But we had no idea what was going on.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'The doctors were asking, did he do any drugs? But George was not a risk taker and it could not have been that.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'We found out after three days that it was Meningitis B, and his CT scan had shown he was never going to recover. So after five days, we took the only decision we could - to turn off his life-support machine.'</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">In a helpless moment, the family checked George's vaccination records only to find he was not covered from the disease as they had thought. The vaccine required was not yet available in 2017.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Meningitis had already struck George's school the year before, infecting two girls and killing one. </p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Well Pharmacy's Deputy Superintendent Pharmacist Wendy Lee, warned: 'George's story is tragic, but sadly not an isolated case.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'Although the Men B vaccine is now available free of charge for students from year 13, we are extremely concerned by its current slow uptake.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'The new university term is now just weeks away, and we urge all eligible students to get themselves booked in at their local pharmacy for an injection that might just save their life.'</p><div class="artSplitter mol-img-group" style="style"> <div class="mol-img"> <div class="image-wrap"> <img id="i-969cf63d5ec46709" src="https://i.dailymail.com/1s/2026/09/13/09/111217133-16127457-image-a-7_1789287629046.jpg" height="1074" width="634" alt="George collapsed at the festival after suffering a heart attack and he stopped breathing for 12 minutes. He had catastrophic brain injuries and died in hospital" class="blkBorder img-share" style="max-width:100%" loading="lazy" /> </div> </div> <p class="imageCaption">George collapsed at the festival after suffering a heart attack and he stopped breathing for 12 minutes. He had catastrophic brain injuries and died in hospital</p></div><div class="artSplitter mol-img-group" style="style"> <div class="mol-img"> <div class="image-wrap"> <img id="i-737de2e62ec5e564" src="https://i.dailymail.com/1s/2026/09/13/09/111217041-16127457-image-a-6_1789287617076.jpg" height="951" width="634" alt="Well Pharmacy's Deputy Superintendent Pharmacist Wendy Lee warned: 'George's story is tragic, but sadly not an isolated case.' adding she was 'extremely concerned' with the slow uptake of vaccines" class="blkBorder img-share" style="max-width:100%" loading="lazy" /> </div> </div> <p class="imageCaption">Well Pharmacy's Deputy Superintendent Pharmacist Wendy Lee warned: 'George's story is tragic, but sadly not an isolated case.' adding she was 'extremely concerned' with the slow uptake of vaccines</p></div><p class="mol-para-with-font">The infection attacks the membranes surrounding your brain, inflaming them and putting dangerous pressure on the central nervous system.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Ms Lee said that the bacteria causing it can be carried harmlessly in the throat but can invade the bloodstream and cause meningitis and 'become life-threatening extremely quickly.'</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'Around one in four 15–19-year-olds carry meningococcal bacteria in the back of their throat without knowing it,' she said.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">To protect against the disease, two doses of the vaccine are needed at least four weeks apart. Ms Lee added: 'If you've already had your first, make sure you go back for your second appointment.'</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">There is currently a free NHS MenB catch-up programme offering free shots to teenagers and young adults ahead of the 2026/27 university year. </p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Young people born between 1 September 2007 and 31 August 2008 - the current Year 13 age group - can get it for free, Ms Lee said.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">People born on or after 21 July 2001 who are starting university or certain residential further-education colleges for the first time in autumn 2026 are also eligible.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Nicole echoed her advice, adding: 'You just don't know whether you're going to be one of those people who gets it or not. And in one in 10 cases it can be fatal, just like it was for George.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'It's meningitis season coming up. I wouldn't ever take the risk. It's a very effective vaccination once you have it. And up until the age of 25, you've got a much higher chance to catch it, especially when you're going into university and you're mixing with new people.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'It really scares me that there are people starting university in meningitis season and yet people aren't taking this on.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'Please take some time to go and get vaccinated. Educate yourselves, speak to your GP, your nurses. If you're worried, you've got any questions, educate yourself.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'Don't think you're invincible. Get the jabs and stay safe.'</p><div class="art-ins mol-factbox news" data-version="2" id="mol-98955440-af4a-11f1-b273-fbeb335cc1be" data-permabox-url="https://www.dailymail.com/news/article-16127457/sister-begs-students-menigitis-vaccine.html"> <h3 class="mol-factbox-title">Pharmacist advice and symptoms </h3> <div class="ins cleared mol-factbox-body"> <p class="mol-para-with-font">Pharmacist Wendy Lee is urging Brits to get meninigits B vaccines and to be aware of the signs and symptoms of the disease - as thousands of students prepare to head off to university this month.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Well Pharmacy's Deputy Superintendent Wendy Lee said: 'Meningitis is a terrifying infection. You'll feel seriously unwell very quickly, and it can turn life-threatening within a matter of hours.'</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">A million youngsters in England are eligible for a two-dose vaccination available at local pharmacies as part of an NHS drive.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">The one-off programme was launched following the UK's largest and fastest-growing meningitis B outbreak in Kent this year and two further 'unusual' clusters in Weymouth and the Reading.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">The outbreaks left three teenagers dead - two in Kent and one in Oxfordshire.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Wendy said: 'Starting university means youngsters are meeting lots of new people and often living in close-contact settings such as halls of residence, where infections can spread more easily.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'MenB can become serious very quickly, and vaccination is a simple way to give students and parents peace of mind before they head off to university.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'It's really important to remember that the MenB vaccine requires two doses, given at least four weeks apart. If you've already had your first, make sure you go back for your second appointment.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'The second dose is important to complete the course and give you the best protection, so don't assume that having your first jab means you're fully protected.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">'If you're heading off to university, check when your second dose is due and make sure you get it booked in.'</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Meningitis is an inflammation of the protective membranes around the brain and spinal cord. While viral meningitis is more common, bacterial forms are less common but can be far more serious.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">One of the main causes is meningococcal group B (MenB), which can cause both meningitis and sepsis, both of which can become life-threatening within hours.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">According to the latest UK Health Security Agency figures, there were 313 confirmed cases of MenB in England in 2024/25, accounting for 82.6% of all invasive meningococcal disease cases.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Overall, invasive meningococcal disease killed 31 people between 2024 - 2025.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">According to NHS guidance, Meningococcal disease is fatal in around one in 10 cases.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font"><span class="mol-style-bold">Symptoms </span></p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Early symptoms can look deceptively similar to flu, including a high temperature, headache, vomiting, muscle and joint pain and feeling generally unwell.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">But warning signs include a stiff neck, dislike of bright lights, confusion, breathing quickly, cold hands and feet, seizures, or becoming very sleepy and difficult to wake.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">A rash can be a key warning sign, particularly one that does not fade when pressed, but waiting for a rash to appear is dangerous because it may not develop early, or even at all.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Wendy said: 'If someone has a stiff neck, a dislike of bright lights, or is becoming confused and difficult to wake, these are serious red flags. Seek immediate emergency help, do not wait for a rash to appear.'</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Anyone who suspects meningitis or meningococcal disease should seek emergency medical help immediately by calling 999 or going to A&E.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Bacterial meningococcal disease requires urgent hospital treatment, including intravenous antibiotics and fluids.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">The consequences of surviving can also be severe. MenB can cause hearing loss, brain damage, seizures and problems with memory and concentration, while meningococcal sepsis can result in tissue damage and amputations.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">Well pharmacists can provide advice on the signs and symptoms of meningitis, when to seek urgent medical care and whether patients are eligible for the free NHS MenB vaccination.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">The MenB jab is available at participating Well Pharmacies in England. Patients can check eligibility, find their nearest branch and book an appointment through the Well website now.</p><p class="mol-para-with-font">For Wendy, her message is simple: 'Don't wait and see. With meningitis, acting quickly could be the difference between life and death.'</p> </div> </div></div><div class="linkButtonRow articleTopicsRow " data-track-module="article-topics-row"><a class="linkButtonRowItem" href="/news/bristol/index.html?ico=article_topics_module">Bristol</a></div>

Prince William will not have an awkward moment facing brother Harry at Lady Amelia Windsor's wedding because one of them is not on the guest list Previous Next 'My brother was going to his first festival when he felt tired - days later we were turning off his life support': Grieving sister begs students to get meningitis B jab after bug killed 18-year-old See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source By JAKE HOLDEN, UK NEWS REPORTER Published: 09:36 BST, 13 September 2026 | Updated: 09:41 BST, 13 September 2026 e-mail 29 View comments --> --> --> The grieving sister of an 18-year-old sixth form student killed by meningitis B has issued a plea begging others to get vaccinated against the deadly disease. Nicole Zographou's baby brother George had excitedly set off to the Boardmasters surf and music festival in Newquay, but told his sister he was feeling ill beforehand. Undeterred and determined to enjoy himself, young George and his friend drove off from Bristol, but on the journey his condition worsened. He developed a pain in his foot and became increasingly woozy. Overnight, he began uncontrollably vomiting and could no longer walk by morning. Unbeknownst to him, a meningococcal infection was ripping through his body at terrifying speed. Hours later, he collapsed, suffering a heart attack and a catastrophic brain injury. He was rushed to hospital, where he was found to be a victim of meningitis B - a vicious bug which cruelly targets teenagers and young adults. Five days on, his family was forced to make the brutal decision to turn off his life support. Sparkly-eyed, kind, funny, beautiful George was dead. Nicole, 38, said: 'He died in his peak. If George hadn't got meningitis B, he would be with us today. He would be 28, enjoying a good career, having finished university, and still be having fun. Nicole Zographou said her 18-year-old brother's death from meningitis B 'has bled into every part of my life.' She added: 'We were really close, and I miss him incredibly' Nicole, a senior public health practitioner, urged young people to get vaccinated. She said: 'Please check. Please ask. Please have the jabs and get protected. Please don't make the mistake of thinking this won't happen to you.' 'His death has bled into every part of my life. We were really close, and I miss him incredibly. I'd give the world to have him back.' The coroner's reports stated that the only thing that would have saved George's life would have been a vaccination, senior public health practitioner Nicole said. She issued an urgent warning for students to get vaccinated ahead of the return to university later this month. In a desperate plea, she added: 'Please check. Please ask. Please have the jabs and get protected. Please don't make the mistake of thinking this won't happen to you.' In March, two students aged 18 and 21 were killed by meningitis B in an outbreak in Kent which infected 21 people following a fateful club night out . Another 18-year-old was killed in Oxfordshire by the disease in May. Last week, the teenagers in Suffolk were rushed to hospital with the same infection. Nicole spoke further about her brother's death in 2017: 'George felt a little unwell. Five days later he was dead. That is how quickly this disease can take hold. 'You cannot look at a healthy 18-year-old and imagine that they could be dead within days. That's what is so frightening about meningitis. 'It can start with symptoms that seem ordinary, and you might not realise how seriously ill someone is until they suddenly deteriorate so quickly that they cannot be treated.' George Zographou said he had been feeling mildly ill before he set off to Boardmasters festival in 2017. Five days later his family were forced to shut off his life support after he was struck down by meningitis Nicole said: 'There were four of us in our happy family. Now we’re like a three-legged chair and we don’t really function very well any more without him' Nicole added: 'The coroner's report said the only thing that would have saved him was a vaccination. That's what it said on his on his death report.' Nicole painfully recalled the day she last saw her brother - a student at St Brendon's Sixth Form College in Bristol - before he was struck down by meningitis. George was excited - excited for his first festival experience, even excited by the journey, having never driven on a motorway before. She said: 'He told me he was feeling a little unwell and I advised him not to push himself. I told him to make sure he sought help if he needed it, but he wasn't feeling too bad, so none of us were too worried.' Nicole was jetting off to Ibiza for a week on her own adventure, which she had been really looking forward to as well. So they said their goodbyes and parted ways. Soon after arriving in Newquay, George was texting their parents -mum Elaine, now 73, and dad Andrew Zographou, now 59 - and Snapchatting Nicole in Ibiza to tell them he had started feeling very unwell. The following evening, a call came that changed the family forever. George had gone into cardiac arrest and stopped breathing for 12 minutes. Nicole said: 'From the call, I learned he'd been blue-lighted to hospital, placed on life support and was found to have suffered a catastrophic brain injury.' She rushed back home, getting the first flight back from Ibiza and arrived 10 hours later at her brother's side, where he was being kept alive with a life support machine. Nicole continued: 'He was catastrophically brain dead. But we had no idea what was going on. 'The doctors were asking, did he do any drugs? But George was not a risk taker and it could not have been that. 'We found out after three days that it was Meningitis B, and his CT scan had shown he was never going to recover. So after five days, we took the only decision we could - to turn off his life-support machine.' In a helpless moment, the family checked George's vaccination records only to find he was not covered from the disease as they had thought. The vaccine required was not yet available in 2017. Meningitis had already struck George's school the year before, infecting two girls and killing one. Well Pharmacy's Deputy Superintendent Pharmacist Wendy Lee, warned: 'George's story is tragic, but sadly not an isolated case. 'Although the Men B vaccine is now available free of charge for students from year 13, we are extremely concerned by its current slow uptake. 'The new university term is now just weeks away, and we urge all eligible students to get themselves booked in at their local pharmacy for an injection that might just save their life.' George collapsed at the festival after suffering a heart attack and he stopped breathing for 12 minutes. He had catastrophic brain injuries and died in hospital Well Pharmacy's Deputy Superintendent Pharmacist Wendy Lee warned: 'George's story is tragic, but sadly not an isolated case.' adding she was 'extremely concerned' with the slow uptake of vaccines The infection attacks the membranes surrounding your brain, inflaming them and putting dangerous pressure on the central nervous system. Ms Lee said that the bacteria causing it can be carried harmlessly in the throat but can invade the bloodstream and cause meningitis and 'become life-threatening extremely quickly.' 'Around one in four 15–19-year-olds carry meningococcal bacteria in the back of their throat without knowing it,' she said. To protect against the disease, two doses of the vaccine are needed at least four weeks apart. Ms Lee added: 'If you've already had your first, make sure you go back for your second appointment.' There is currently a free NHS MenB catch-up programme offering free shots to teenagers and young adults ahead of the 2026/27 university year. Young people born between 1 September 2007 and 31 August 2008 - the current Year 13 age group - can get it for free, Ms Lee said. People born on or after 21 July 2001 who are starting university or certain residential further-education colleges for the first time in autumn 2026 are also eligible. Nicole echoed her advice, adding: 'You just don't know whether you're going to be one of those people who gets it or not. And in one in 10 cases it can be fatal, just like it was for George. 'It's meningitis season coming up. I wouldn't ever take the risk. It's a very effective vaccination once you have it. And up until the age of 25, you've got a much higher chance to catch it, especially when you're going into university and you're mixing with new people. 'It really scares me that there are people starting university in meningitis season and yet people aren't taking this on. 'Please take some time to go and get vaccinated. Educate yourselves, speak to your GP, your nurses. If you're worried, you've got any questions, educate yourself. 'Don't think you're invincible. Get the jabs and stay safe.' Pharmacist advice and symptoms Pharmacist Wendy Lee is urging Brits to get meninigits B vaccines and to be aware of the signs and symptoms of the disease - as thousands of students prepare to head off to university this month. Well Pharmacy's Deputy Superintendent Wendy Lee said: 'Meningitis is a terrifying infection. You'll feel seriously unwell very quickly, and it can turn life-threatening within a matter of hours.' A million youngsters in England are eligible for a two-dose vaccination available at local pharmacies as part of an NHS drive. The one-off programme was launched following the UK's largest and fastest-growing meningitis B outbreak in Kent this year and two further 'unusual' clusters in Weymouth and the Reading. The outbreaks left three teenagers dead - two in Kent and one in Oxfordshire. Wendy said: 'Starting university means youngsters are meeting lots of new people and often living in close-contact settings such as halls of residence, where infections can spread more easily. 'MenB can become serious very quickly, and vaccination is a simple way to give students and parents peace of mind before they head off to university. 'It's really important to remember that the MenB vaccine requires two doses, given at least four weeks apart. If you've already had your first, make sure you go back for your second appointment. 'The second dose is important to complete the course and give you the best protection, so don't assume that having your first jab means you're fully protected. 'If you're heading off to university, check when your second dose is due and make sure you get it booked in.' Meningitis is an inflammation of the protective membranes around the brain and spinal cord. While viral meningitis is more common, bacterial forms are less common but can be far more serious. One of the main causes is meningococcal group B (MenB), which can cause both meningitis and sepsis, both of which can become life-threatening within hours. According to the latest UK Health Security Agency figures, there were 313 confirmed cases of MenB in England in 2024/25, accounting for 82.6% of all invasive meningococcal disease cases. Overall, invasive meningococcal disease killed 31 people between 2024 - 2025. According to NHS guidance, Meningococcal disease is fatal in around one in 10 cases. Symptoms Early symptoms can look deceptively similar to flu, including a high temperature, headache, vomiting, muscle and joint pain and feeling generally unwell. But warning signs include a stiff neck, dislike of bright lights, confusion, breathing quickly, cold hands and feet, seizures, or becoming very sleepy and difficult to wake. A rash can be a key warning sign, particularly one that does not fade when pressed, but waiting for a rash to appear is dangerous because it may not develop early, or even at all. Wendy said: 'If someone has a stiff neck, a dislike of bright lights, or is becoming confused and difficult to wake, these are serious red flags. Seek immediate emergency help, do not wait for a rash to appear.' Anyone who suspects meningitis or meningococcal disease should seek emergency medical help immediately by calling 999 or going to A&E. Bacterial meningococcal disease requires urgent hospital treatment, including intravenous antibiotics and fluids. The consequences of surviving can also be severe. MenB can cause hearing loss, brain damage, seizures and problems with memory and concentration, while meningococcal sepsis can result in tissue damage and amputations. Well pharmacists can provide advice on the signs and symptoms of meningitis, when to seek urgent medical care and whether patients are eligible for the free NHS MenB vaccination. The MenB jab is available at participating Well Pharmacies in England. Patients can check eligibility, find their nearest branch and book an appointment through the Well website now. For Wendy, her message is simple: 'Don't wait and see. With meningitis, acting quickly could be the difference between life and death.' If you make a purchase via links on this page we will earn commission - learn more If a festive ski getaway is at the top of your winter wishlist then Club Med’s limited-time sale September Winter Sale has you covered. Ideal for family trips and couples breaks alike, the all-inclusive travel company are reducing the price of ski holidays by up to £600 per person in its unmissable sale, helping you save big on unforgettable ski holidays in an array of stunning resorts. What's more, it also includes ski passes and lessons for all levels with accommodation, dining, activities and more in one seamless package Les Arcs Panorama Highly rated, the Les Arcs Panorama is nestled in a clearing at 1,750 metres of the Les Arcs 1600 ski area of Paradiski®. Named after its panoramic views, this all-inclusive ski resort hidden among pine trees is perfect for families, with kids’ ski classes and playful animal sculptures dotted about our chic restaurants and lounges. From £1,414 Shop The perfect excuse to start planning your festive trip, Club Med’s ski holiday deals are here to make a premium festive getaway that much more affordable Skiing holidays can quickly become an expensive affair once you factor in accommodation, lift passes, equipment, lessons and everything else you need for a week on the slopes. For shoppers after a more affordable option for Christmas and New Year breaks, Club Med’s September sale could make booking your next winter escape a little easier, with savings of up to £600 per person across selected ski holidays. Running from September 1 to 15, the sale is the perfect excuse to start planning your festive trip, supplying you with everything you need to enjoy an adrenaline-filled trip for less. RELATED ARTICLES Previous 1 Next The fragrance advent calendar that sold out two years... The affordable George at Asda coats we're eyeing up for the... Share this article Share Designed to take the stress out of organising a ski trip, the brand’s premium all-inclusive resorts offer everything you need under one roof, from accommodation and dining to ski passes, lessons and a host of activities. Better still, many of its resorts are ski-in, ski-out, meaning you can step straight out of the resort and onto the slopes without the usual morning trek or complicated transfers. Ski passes are also included in the packages, helping you avoid the additional cost and hassle of arranging them separately. A bit rusty on the slopes or skiing for the first time? Ski lessons are also included for all ability levels, ideal if you need a quick reminder before strapping on your skis. The brand’s premium all-inclusive resorts offer everything you need under one roof, from accommodation and dining to ski passes, lessons and a host of activities From the moment you arrive, your accommodation, meals, ski passes, lessons and activities are taken care of, making Club Med a brilliant hack for busy shoppers. Club Med’s luxury all-inclusive holiday experiences are still available for a range of dreamy destinations over the festive period, including its most searched-for resorts like the Alp d' Huez and the Les Arcs Panorama in France – but you’ll have to book fast. These incredible September Winter Sale savings will end on September 15 and dates are booking up fast, so be sure to book your next trip sooner rather than later. Club Med September Winter Sale highlights Alpe d'Huez Savoie, in the French Alps, hosts some of the world's most famous ski areas, and the Alpe d'Huez is a great option for all ski levels. You could tackle the 16km Sarenne, Europe's longest ski run or relax at the Payot Spa, take a yoga class, swim or just enjoy a drink at one of the many bars. From £1,659 Shop Tignes In the centre of the liveliest part of the Tignes ski resort, in Val Claret, the new Club Med Tignes Resort brings a real sparkle to the mountains and offers skiing suited to every skill level. The resort's ambiance is happy and family friendly, right down to the decor where the colours and patterns add pizazz to the traditional mountain features. From £1,357 Shop Val d'Isère Amongst the most stylish and authentic in the Alps, this resort in the magical village of Val d'Isère offers everything that lovers of skiing, fine dining and well-being could possibly want - a spa, pool, yoga and opportunities to unwind. The only Club Med Exclusive Collection Resort to be located in the mountains, this resort offers another definition of luxury, blending privacy, informality and relaxation for all the family against the perfect, snowy backdrop. From £1,549 Shop Val Thorens Sensations With bright balconies, light airy spaces and panoramic alpine views, Club Med Val Thorens Sensations is a chic all-inclusive ski resort with a fun contemporary feel. At 2,300 metres, this is one of ClubMed's highest altitude ski hotels, with a ski lift right at the centre of the resort ready to take you into the Three Valleys domain.
